title: Past Questions: Module One
lead: Every past question whose answerable parts are Module One, filed by module rather than by year, most repeated first, with the course text assignments he draws from.
intro:
Past questions only, and nothing else. This is your Question 1 practice: the parts of both papers that sit in Module One of the course text, plus the two tutor marked assignments the examiner draws from.

How to read the label above each question

Every question is here whole and as printed, because that is how you will meet it. The table above each one says, part by part, which module it belongs to and whether you answer it. The line under that names every other paper where the same thing was set.

Order is by repetition, not by year. The clothing line assignment is first because he set it as a paper question almost word for word.

lockin.big: "Module One has no diagrams, so every mark is a named list tied to a phrase in the scenario. Identify, justify, outline."
lockin.sub: Methodology choice, the analyst’s eight steps, the analyst’s skills and the SDLC phases are the four families he keeps returning to. Learn those four and Question 1 is answered.

questions.heading: The course text’s clothing line assignment, the one he lifted

scenario.src: Course text, Module One Unit 3, page 43
scenario.tag: Course text, Module One Unit 3, page 43, a tutor marked assignment
scenario.text:
You are the chosen project manager for a new clothing line about to be launched. You very much need the project to succeed and are willing to give it your all.
1. Outline and discuss five skills you must possess to make the project flourish.
2. Define the scope of the project, state activities to be conducted, and give a detailed outline of the timeline of your project (for the space of six months)
3. What are those criteria you will need to select good team members? List and explain 4 most important ones to you.
4. The requirements of this work MAY NOT be clearly stated at the beginning. Choose an appropriate SDLC methodology and map the project’s phases.
5. You are nearing the end of the project, and the client is insisting on adding new features, but you want to prevent scope and feature creep. Do you refuse or agree to add the new features? Give three cogent reasons for your decision as PM.

questions.asked:
This is the strongest repeat evidence you have. The examiner set this assignment as 2024/2025 Q1(c) almost word for word: same project manager, same unclear requirements, same client demanding features near the end, same three cogent reasons. Work it here, then compare it with that paper question.

5 of 5 parts are yours.

PartModuleOn your planWhat it asks
(1)Module OneAnswer itFive skills a project manager needs
(2)Module OneAnswer itScope, activities and a six month timeline
(3)Module OneAnswer itFour criteria for selecting team members
(4)Module OneAnswer itChoose a methodology for unclear requirements and map the phases
(5)Module OneAnswer itRefuse or agree to late features, with three reasons

breakdown.question: Work this in your book before you open anything. What is given, what is asked, and what would earn nothing?
breakdown.answer: Work it first Write the full answer in your book, then mark yourself against the model below.

exam.problem: Answer the assignment above in full in your book, then open this.
exam.answer:
Methodology. Requirements unclear at the start points straight at the selection criterion clarity of user requirements, and the manual's answer there is system prototyping or throwaway prototyping, because they provide prototypes for users to interact with early in the SDLC. Since a clothing line also implies visual design that people must react to rather than describe, evolutionary prototyping fits: build an initial version, refine it through continuous user feedback until it becomes the final product.

Phases mapped. A preliminary project plan; a partial high-level model as a source for partial requirements; a prototype built with the basic and critical attributes; the designer builds the database, user interface and algorithmic functions; demonstrate, the user evaluates and suggests improvements; loop until satisfied, then bring the prototype up to product standard.

On the late feature request. Either answer can score, provided the reasons are the manual's. A defensible refusal:

  • Scope creep is a named risk of exactly this methodology. The manual lists among prototyping's disadvantages that the process may continue forever due to scope creep, and that user expectations may increase and requirements expand during the project.
  • There is a risk of never achieving closure, since user expectations cannot be totally managed. Accepting late features feeds that risk directly.
  • The principle allows revising scope deliberately, not drifting into it. Do not be afraid to cancel or revise scope is about a controlled decision when a project is too costly or misaligned, which is not the same as absorbing requests near delivery.

A defensible acceptance would cite the incremental model instead: accept the features into a LATER increment, since further requirements analysis can still be performed for later increments, while changes for the current increment cannot be accepted. That answer scores because it names the mechanism rather than just saying yes.

frames.teach: Every methodology question on either paper has the same three moves, whatever the scenario: identify an approach, justify it against the words in front of you, outline what the work would look like. Nothing else earns marks.
frames.ask: This assignment says the requirements MAY NOT be clearly stated at the beginning. What does that one clause rule out?

frames.check: Every predictive method, because a predictive approach fixes requirements upfront.
frames.teach: Methods split into two families, and the exam wants the split by name. Predictive: requirements defined upfront, a linear sequence, heavy documentation, limited flexibility for change. Adaptive: requirements evolve, iterative and incremental, strong user involvement, working software over documentation.
frames.ask: So which family, and name two methods inside it?

frames.check: Adaptive: Agile, and either RAD or system prototyping.
frames.teach: Now the six selection criteria, which is the single most examined table in Module One: clarity of user requirements, familiarity with technology, system complexity, system reliability, short time schedules, schedule visibility. Unclear requirements point at prototyping; unfamiliar technology at throwaway prototyping; a short schedule at RAD.
frames.ask: You have named Agile. Out of the marks for this part, how much is the naming worth?

frames.check: Almost none. The marks are in the justification.
frames.teach: So justify by quoting the scenario back, clause by clause, and answering each clause with a feature: requirements not clear at the start, answered by requirements that evolve iteration by iteration; a client who will want changes, answered by each iteration ending in a working increment and a review.
frames.ask: Part 5 asks whether you refuse or agree to late features. Is there a right answer?

frames.check: No, but there is a right SHAPE: take a position, then give three reasons tied to the project.
frames.teach: The examiner is testing judgement, not obedience. A strong answer agrees to add them into a later iteration or release rather than the current one, which is the incremental model's own rule: further analysis is allowed for LATER increments, but changes to the CURRENT one are not accepted. That is what keeps an increment finishable.
frames.ask: And one habit is left, worth the last mark on any methodology answer anywhere. What have you not done?

frames.check: Named the alternative you rejected, and why.
frames.teach: Close with two lines: "Waterfall was rejected: it requires requirements to be clear and stable throughout, it is difficult to respond to change, and the customer sees nothing until it may be too late." That sentence is the difference between a pass and a good mark, and it costs ten seconds.

questions.heading: The course text’s retail company assignment

scenario.text:
1. Explain the Planning and Analysis phases of the System Development Life Cycle (SDLC), highlighting their objectives and key activities.
2. A medium-sized retail company wants to develop a new online sales and inventory management system. The company expects frequent changes in customer requirements, plans to introduce new features regularly, and seeks continuous user feedback throughout development. As a systems analyst,
a) Identify the most suitable software development approach for this project.
b) Justify your choice by explaining how the selected approach addresses the company’s needs.
c) Outline the key activities that would be carried out using this approach during system development.

questions.asked:
The same shape as every methodology question on both papers: a scenario, then identify, justify and outline. Its first part, explaining the Planning and Analysis phases, is the same family as 2024/2025 Q2(a) and 2025/2026 Q5(b).

4 of 4 parts are yours.

PartModuleOn your planWhat it asks
(1)Module OneAnswer itThe Planning and Analysis phases, objectives and activities
(2a)Module OneAnswer itIdentify the most suitable approach
(2b)Module OneAnswer itJustify it against the company’s stated needs
(2c)Module OneAnswer itOutline the key activities

The method is taught in this section. Work the frames under the clothing line assignment at the top of this paper, then come back and write this one against the clock.

breakdown.question: Work this in your book before you open anything. What is given, what is asked, and what would earn nothing?
breakdown.answer: The manual’s own version A medium-sized retail company wants to develop a new online sales and inventory management system. The company expects frequent changes in customer requirements, plans to introduce new features regularly, and seeks continuous user feedback throughout development. As a systems analyst: (a) identify the most suitable software development approach; (b) justify your choice; (c) outline the key activities that would be carried out using this approach.

exam.problem: Answer the assignment above in full in your book, then open this.
exam.answer:
Step 1: underline the scenario's signals before choosing anything. There are three, and the examiner put them there deliberately.

The scenario saysWhich criterion that is
"expects frequent changes in customer requirements"Requirements are unstable, so a predictive approach is ruled out
"plans to introduce new features regularly"Delivery must be incremental, not one big release
"seeks continuous user feedback throughout development"The user will be involved throughout the life cycle

Step 2: (a) identify. The ADAPTIVE approach, specifically an Agile methodology. Say both: the family and the member. If you prefer, RAD is defensible for the same reasons; what is not defensible is Waterfall or the V-model.

Step 3: (b) justify, phrase by phrase. This is the part worth writing carefully.

  • The company expects frequent changes. An adaptive approach assumes the project cannot be planned in full in advance and must be modified as it progresses, so change is accommodated by design rather than treated as a problem. A predictive approach defines requirements upfront and has limited flexibility to accommodate change, which is the opposite of what this company needs.
  • The company plans to introduce new features regularly. Agile works in short time-boxed sprints, each ending with a working increment of the system delivered for evaluation, so new features reach users continuously rather than waiting for a single delivery at the end.
  • The company seeks continuous user feedback. The adaptive approach is built on strong user involvement and collaboration, with requirements captured as user stories and prioritised by business value and urgency, and a sprint review and retrospective closing each cycle.
  • Retail is a dynamic business environment. The manual notes explicitly that adaptive approaches suit dynamic environments requiring flexibility and rapid response to change, while predictive approaches suit stable, well-understood requirements.

Step 4: (c) outline the key activities. Use the manual's adaptive phases, and name them.

  1. Initiation and requirements planning. Define high-level scope: the business problem, overall objectives, key stakeholders, major features. Detailed requirements are deliberately not fully specified. Requirements are captured at a high level as user stories and prioritised by business value and urgency.
  2. Iterative analysis and design. Only the requirements selected for the current iteration are analysed and designed in detail.
  3. Iterative development or construction. Components are built in short cycles, each producing a working, testable piece of the system.
  4. Continuous testing and quality assurance. Testing runs throughout rather than at the end, so defects are detected and corrected early.

Then, per sprint: create and prioritise user stories, plan the sprint and assign tasks, develop and test within the sprint, and hold a sprint review and retrospective.

How to earn the last few marks

Add one sentence saying what you would NOT do and why: a predictive approach such as Waterfall was rejected because its requirements are fixed upfront and it offers little opportunity for the customer to preview the system until it may be too late.

Showing the rejected alternative demonstrates the judgement the question is testing.

exam.problem: Write your answer to PQ 24/25 Q2 in your book first, one clear point for every mark. Then open the model answer and mark yourself against it.
exam.answer:
Answer · PQ 24/25 Q2

a. Four phases: objectives and activities (8 marks)

Analysis: objective, understand and document what the system must do; activities, gather information, define and prioritise requirements, build prototypes, evaluate alternatives. Design: objective, specify how it will be built; activities, design the architecture, network, interfaces, database and controls. Implementation: objective, a reliable working system with trained users; activities, construct, test, convert data, train and document, install. Support: objective, keep it running for years; activities, maintain, enhance, support the users (help desk).

b. Three stakeholders (3 marks)

Users want it easy and helpful for daily work; managers want business value on time and on budget; developers want clear requirements and a feasible, maintainable system.

c. Tools versus techniques (4 marks)

A tool is a software product used to do the work; a technique is a way of completing one activity. Tools: a modelling package, an IDE. Techniques: interviewing, cost-benefit analysis.

d. Key business information for XYZ (2.5 marks)

The business goals and processes, the people and their roles, the data the business keeps, the existing systems and their weaknesses, and the rules and constraints the new system must respect.

frames.teach: This question wants the life cycle as a table in your head: for each phase, its objective, its activities, its deliverables. Write it that way in the hall and the marks are countable.
frames.ask: Name the five phases of the SDLC in order, before the answer names four of them.

frames.teach: Note what the question did: it named a four phased cycle, analysis, design, implementation and support, leaving Planning out. Answer the question as asked, and add one line saying the text also treats Planning as a phase. Never correct the examiner silently, and never ignore his wording.

frames.check: Identify the scope, ensure the project is feasible, and produce a schedule, resource plan and budget.
frames.teach: Its five activities: define the problem, produce the schedule, confirm feasibility, staff the project, launch the project. Feasibility is confirmed in Planning, in five kinds: economic, organisational, technical, resource, schedule. That trap is asked constantly.
frames.ask: Analysis is next. What one word does the text use for what Analysis is?

frames.teach: Analysis establishes WHAT the system must do, never HOW. Six activities: gather information, define requirements, prioritise requirements, build a prototype for discovery, generate and evaluate alternatives, review recommendations with management. Design then answers HOW, in five activities: application architecture, network, user and system interfaces, database, system controls.
frames.ask: Implementation includes the changeover. What are the four ways to switch over?

frames.check: Direct cutover, parallel, phased and pilot.
frames.teach: Phased splits the SYSTEM, pilot splits the USERS: that pair is confused constantly. Support is the last phase, and its three activities are maintain, enhance and support the users through a help desk.
frames.ask: Part (b) asks for three stakeholders and how each views a system. Who are they?

frames.check: Users, management and technical staff, in the text's terms.
frames.teach: The point is that each sees a different system: the user sees the work it helps them do, management sees a capital investment to be justified against costs and risks, and the technical staff see something to be built, integrated and maintained. Part (c) is the tools against techniques pair: tools are software products, techniques are strategies for completing an activity.

questions.heading: 2025/2026, Question Five: the federal teaching hospital

scenario.text: A federal teaching hospital intends to replace its fragmented patient appointment, clinical record, laboratory request, and medication tracking systems with a single integrated Clinical Workflow and Patient Safety Management System. The current system is partly paper-based and partly supported by disconnected departmental applications. Doctors complain that patient records are incomplete, nurses report delays in medication administration, laboratory scientists complain about duplicated test requests, and hospital administrators are concerned about regulatory compliance, audit trails, and data privacy. The hospital's board wants the system delivered within twelve months. However, stakeholders disagree on system priorities. Doctors want speed and flexibility, nurses want ease of use, laboratory staff want accurate workflow integration, and administrators insist on strict documentation, traceability, and reliability. Failure in the new system could affect patient safety. a. Briefly compare seven (7) methodologies that can be used in this project. (7 mks) [Hint: your answer should be short and concisely state why the methodologies may be suitable or not] b. Identify five (5) activities in project planning. (5 mks) c. Using the case, formulate at least: i. two (2) business requirements, ii. two (2) user requirements, iii. three (3) functional requirements, iv. two (2) non-functional requirements, and v. two (2) system requirements, (5.5 mks)

questions.asked:

3 of 3 parts are yours.

PartModuleOn your planWhat it asks
(a)Module OneAnswer itCompare seven methodologies, saying briefly why each suits this project or does not
(b)Module OneAnswer itFive activities in project planning
(c)Module TwoAnswer itFormulate business, user, functional, non functional and system requirements

The method is taught in this section. Work the frames under the clothing line assignment at the top of this paper, then come back and write this one against the clock.

exam.problem: Write your answer to PQ 25/26 Q5 in your book first, one clear point for every mark. Then open the model answer and mark yourself against it.
exam.answer:
Answer · PQ 25/26 Q5

a. Compare seven methodologies (7 marks)

  • Waterfall: strong documentation and traceability suit a safety-critical system, but its rigidity is risky if requirements shift.
  • Prototyping: good for the unclear priorities here, but the prototype can be mistaken for the finished safety system.
  • RAD: fast, which suits the twelve-month deadline, but weak for a large, complex, safety-critical hospital system.
  • Spiral: its risk analysis each cycle fits a safety-critical project well, but it is heavy and slow.
  • Incremental: delivers working pieces early, useful given the deadline, but integration across departments must be managed.
  • Agile: handles the disagreeing stakeholders through constant feedback, but its light documentation clashes with the audit-trail requirement.
  • V-shape: pairs each stage with its test, excellent for the reliability and traceability a hospital demands, but as rigid as waterfall.
Answer, continued

b. Five project planning activities (5 marks)

Define the problem; produce the project schedule; confirm feasibility; staff the project; and launch the project.

c. Formulate requirements (5.5 marks)

  • Business: cut medication-administration delays; achieve regulatory compliance with full audit trails.
  • User: a nurse can administer and record medication at the bedside; a doctor can see a complete patient record in one place.
  • Functional: the system shall record each patient appointment; the system shall flag duplicated laboratory test requests; the system shall log every change to a record for audit.
  • Non-functional: the system shall be available 99.9% of the time; the system shall encrypt all patient data (privacy).
  • System: the system shall store records as time-stamped entries linked to a patient ID; the system shall integrate with the existing departmental applications.

questions.heading: 2025/2026, Question Three: Tikki Tikka and the Boys

They hired Billy Butcher as their analyst to guide them on the steps to take in order to make their automation a success, they also hired a graphic designer and a JavaScript programmer to join the team; they call themselves the Boys. a. Briefly explain the THREE questions that the Boys will need to answer during the Feasibility Analysis phase of their system planning (3 mks) b. Billy's first approach to problem solving is Research and Understand the Problem. Outline any other six (6) steps he can take (3 mks) c. A model is a representation of an important aspect of the real world. How can the Boys properly explain what a model is to the stakeholders? (4 mks) d. The most important skill Billy can have is People knowledge and skill; explain in detail any other skill he can possess to do a great job (3 mks) e. Billy needs to ensure there is adequate support for the users of the new system. What three activities will the support group need to participate in? (3 mks) f. Mention any three other job roles that Billy can fit into (1.5 mks)

breakdown.answer:
Given A food business automating, with an analyst (Billy) and a small team.

Asked Six short written parts, all straight recall from Modules One and Six: feasibility, the problem-solving steps, what a model is, the analyst's skills, support activities and job roles.

Watch Each part names the exact list it wants. Answer the number asked (three questions, six steps, three activities, three roles) and no more.

exam.problem: Write your answer to PQ 25/26 Q3 in your book first, one clear point for every mark. Then open the model answer and mark yourself against it.
exam.answer:
Answer · PQ 25/26 Q3

a. Three feasibility questions (3 marks)

Feasibility analysis asks whether the project is worth pursuing, from three angles: Is it technically feasible? (do we have the technology and skill to build it?); Is it economically feasible? (do the benefits outweigh the costs?); and Is it operationally feasible? (will the users accept and use it, and does it fit the business?). Schedule and legal feasibility complete the five, but these three are the core questions.

b. Six more problem-solving steps (3 marks)

After researching and understanding the problem: verify the benefits outweigh the costs; define the requirements; develop alternative solutions; recommend the best solution; define the details of the chosen solution; implement it (and then monitor the results).

c. Explaining what a model is (4 marks)

Tell the stakeholders a model is a simplified picture of the system that leaves out detail so everyone can see and agree the important parts before it is built, the way an architect's drawing lets a client approve a building before a brick is laid. The use case diagram, DFD and class diagram they will be shown are all such models.

d. Another skill (3 marks)

Besides people skills, Billy needs technical knowledge and skills: an understanding of computers, networks, databases and the tools and techniques of system building, so he can understand and communicate technical requirements even though the programmer writes the code. (Business knowledge is an equally acceptable answer.)

e. Three support activities (3 marks)

Maintain the system (fix bugs and make minor adjustments); enhance the system (add capability as the business grows); and support the users, which includes running a help desk.

f. Three other job roles (1.5 marks)

Project manager, software architect, and product designer (also acceptable: software tester, business analyst).

frames.teach: Six parts, all Module One, all list questions. The technique for the whole question is the same: name the list, then tie one clause of it to the scenario. The Boys are automating a food business in Nigeria, so every answer can name food, orders or the shop.
frames.ask: Part (a) asks the three questions feasibility analysis answers. What do you think they are?

frames.check: Is it worth doing, can it be done, and can it be done in the time and with what we have.
frames.teach: In the text's own terms: economic, do the benefits outweigh the costs; technical, are the technology and skills available; and organisational or operational, will the business accept and use it. The text also lists resource and schedule feasibility, so name five if the marks allow.
frames.ask: Part (b): the first step of the analyst's approach is research and understand the problem. Name the other seven.

frames.check: Verify the benefits outweigh the costs, define the requirements, develop alternatives, decide and recommend, define the details, implement, monitor.
frames.teach: Eight in all, and the question asks for six more, so the two extra you have are insurance against one you cannot remember. Step 1 has three named parts the examiner asks for by name: who is involved, what business processes come into play, and what other systems would be affected.
frames.ask: Part (c) asks how to explain to stakeholders what a model is. What IS a model, in the text's words?

frames.check: A representation of an important aspect of the real world.
frames.teach: So explain it by naming the aspect it leaves out: a DFD models what the system does with data and says nothing about screens; an ERD models the nouns and nothing about order. Use an analogy they already trust, a floor plan of their shop, and say that a model is cheap to change while a built system is not.
frames.ask: Part (d) says the most important skill is people knowledge. Name the other two kinds, and pick one to explain.

frames.teach: Technical: computers and how they work, storage, input and output, networks and protocols, programming languages and operating systems, and collaboration technology. Business: what business functions organisations perform, how they are structured and managed, and about this company in particular, what it does and what makes it successful. Either earns the marks if you give the detail.
frames.ask: Part (e): the support group's three activities?

frames.check: Maintain the system, enhance it, and support the users.
frames.teach: Maintenance is fixing bugs and small adjustments; enhancement is the bigger changes from new regulations, the market or new infrastructure; support is the help desk, staff available for any technical or processing problem. Part (f), the analyst's other job roles, comes from the seven responsibilities: requirements analyst, system evaluator, feasibility assessor, modeller and documenter, liaison, solution recommender, implementation support.

exam.problem: Write your answer to PQ 24/25 Q5 in your book first, one clear point for every mark. Then open the model answer and mark yourself against it.
exam.answer:
Answer · PQ 24/25 Q5

a. Three skills (7 marks)

Technical: understanding of computers, networks, databases and the tools of building, so the analyst can understand and communicate technical requirements. Business: understanding of how organisations work and what this business does, so the system fits real goals. People (interpersonal): the most important; communicating in interviews and reviews, managing expectations and resolving conflict, because the analyst depends on users, managers and programmers.

b. Hospital class diagram (5 marks)

Classes PATIENT, PATIENTDETAILS, NEWPATIENT, OLDPATIENT, WARD, WARDDETAILS, CONVENIENCEROOM, NURSE. PATIENT is composed of one PATIENTDETAILS (filled diamond, 1); NEWPATIENT and OLDPATIENT generalise to PATIENT (hollow triangle); WARD holds 8..* PATIENTs; WARD is composed of one WARDDETAILS; CONVENIENCEROOM is part of WARD (filled diamond); WARD has 2..* NURSEs. c. Four OOD concepts (4.5 marks)

Polymorphism: the same method behaves differently on different classes (draw() on a Circle versus a Square). Inheritance: a subclass takes on a superclass's members (SavingsAccount from Account). Composition: a life-or-death has-a (a House of Rooms). Aggregation: a loose has-a (a Team of Players).
